readerTitle: When a fix makes the problem worse
caseNote: 실제 연구 (1902년 하노이 쥐 포상금, Michael Vann의 사료 연구; Merton의 개념) + 가상 사례 (배관 수리 회사, 온라인 의류 매장)
insight: 새 규칙은 내 의도가 아니라 그 규칙을 받는 사람이 찾는 가장 쉬운 길로 결과가 정해진다. 그래서 규칙을 만들 때는 '사람들이 어떻게 적응할까'를 먼저 묻는다.
misconception: 규칙이 목표를 분명히 겨냥하고 있으면 결과도 목표대로 나온다. 예상 밖의 결과는 일부 부정직한 사람 때문에 생긴다.

sources.text: Vann, M. G. (2003). Of Rats, Rice, and Race: The Great Hanoi Rat Massacre, an Episode in French Colonial History. French Colonial History, 4, 191–203.
Merton, R. K. (1936). The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action. American Sociological Review, 1(6), 894–904.
배관 수리 회사와 온라인 의류 매장 사례 및 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 하노이 쥐 포상금(1902년, 꼬리를 증거로 제출, 꼬리 없는 쥐 목격, 도시 외곽 쥐 사육 보고, 이후 포상금 폐지)은 Vann(2003) 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 포상금 액수는 자료에 따라 다르게 소개되므로 카드에는 'a small reward'로만 적었습니다. 쥐 사육은 보고 수준이라 'reports of'로 표현했습니다.
Merton(1936)이 의도하지 않은 결과를 체계적으로 다룬 고전 논문이라는 점을 확인하세요. 카드의 세 가지 분류(뜻밖의 이득, 뜻밖의 부작용, 역효과)는 이후 문헌에서 흔히 쓰는 정리이며 Merton 원문의 표현 그대로는 아닙니다. 카드에서 Merton에게 직접 귀속하지 않았습니다.
온라인 의류 매장의 '여러 사이즈를 주문한 뒤 반품하는 행동(bracketing)'은 업계에서 널리 쓰는 관찰이지만 카드의 수치(매출 +15%, 반품 두 배)는 가상입니다.

cards.title: Hanoi paid people to kill rats. Then rats with no tails appeared.
body: In 1902, the French colonial government in Hanoi had a rat problem. Rats carried plague, and the city's new sewers were full of them.
So officials offered residents a small reward for every rat killed. To save themselves from handling bodies, they asked only for the tail as proof.
Soon, people began spotting rats in the streets. Alive, and without tails.

image.label: A rat without a tail running past a pile of coins
image.brief: 20세기 초 하노이 골목을 연상시키는 따뜻한 일러스트. 꼬리 없는 쥐 한 마리가 동전 더미 옆을 달려가고, 뒤쪽에 꼬리가 묶인 다발이 놓인 관청 책상. 실존 인물 얼굴이나 공식 문장은 쓰지 않음. 잔혹한 묘사 없이 가볍게.

cards.title: Your plumbers keep arriving late.
body: You run a plumbing company with 12 technicians. Customers complain that techs show up well after the promised time, and reviews are slipping.
You want on-time arrivals. Which move are you most likely to be glad you made?

options.text: Fine technicians $25 for every arrival more than 15 minutes late
options.feedback: Clear and easy to track. But techs will protect themselves in ways you didn't plan for, and some of those ways cost you more than lateness does.

options.text: Give customers a wider arrival window, like 8 to 12 instead of 9 to 10
options.feedback: Fewer broken promises, quickly. But customers now wait longer, and a rival who promises a tighter window looks better.

options.text: Ask techs why they run late, then add buffer time between jobs and text customers when a tech is on the way
options.feedback: Slower to set up and costs some daily capacity. But it fixes the cause instead of giving people a reason to work around you.

cards.title: The rule worked exactly as written.
body: Residents found the cheapest way to earn. Catch a rat, cut off the tail, let it go. A living rat can breed more rats, which means more tails.
Historian Michael Vann, who studied the colonial records, also found reports of people raising rats outside the city to collect the reward. The program was dropped.
The rule paid for tails. It never paid for fewer rats. **People responded to the rule, not to the goal behind it.**

cards.title: Unintended consequences
body: **Unintended consequences** are results of an action that nobody planned for. Sociologist Robert Merton studied them in a 1936 paper on why purposeful actions so often turn out differently than intended.
They come in three kinds: a surprise benefit, a surprise drawback, and the worst one, a *perverse result*, where the action makes the original problem bigger. Hanoi got the third kind.
The root cause is simple. Any new rule changes what is easy, cheap or rewarded for the people it lands on. They adjust. You planned only for the first effect.

image.label: One action splitting into three paths: benefit, drawback, backfire
image.brief: 가운데 'New rule' 버튼에서 화살표 세 갈래가 뻗어 나감. 'Surprise benefit'(초록), 'Surprise drawback'(노랑), 'Backfire'(빨강, 처음 버튼 쪽으로 되돌아오는 화살표). 깔끔한 플랫 인포그래픽.

cards.title: Picture the $25 fine from the van.
body: Back to the plumbers. Each response below is reasonable for a tech trying to avoid the fine:
list: **Rush the current job** to leave on time, so callbacks rise
**Skip the extra repair** the customer asks about, because it runs long, so revenue drops
**Call ahead to reschedule,** so the visit is never officially late
**Your best tech quits** after paying fines for traffic jams
cards.callout: None of this needs a dishonest person. Just a sensible one.

cards.title: Don't let this freeze you.
body: Every action has consequences you can't fully see, and so does doing nothing. Late plumbers left alone also cost you customers.

The goal isn't to predict everything. Before a change, ask one question: *if I were the person this rule lands on, what is the easiest way to win?* Then roll it out small, decide in advance which side effects you'll watch, and keep it easy to reverse.

cards.title: Now it's an online clothing store.
body: You added free returns to your online store. Sales rose 15%. But returns doubled, and many orders now contain the same jacket in two or three sizes.
Return shipping and repacking are eating the extra profit. What do you do?

options.feedback: Return costs fall fast. But you also lose the hesitant buyers who only ordered because returning was safe, and that was the point of the policy.

options.text: Keep free returns, add better size guides and fit reviews, and track profit per order after returns
options.feedback: This tackles why people order several sizes: they're unsure of fit. It costs effort to build, but you keep the sales gain and measure the side effect directly.

options.text: Offer free returns only on orders over $100
options.feedback: It may cut small returns. But it also invites a new workaround: padding orders past $100, then sending the extras back.

cards.title: People follow the rule, not your intention.
body: Before any new rule, fee, bonus or policy, imagine the person it lands on and find their easiest way to win. That's where the surprises live.
**Try it today:** pick one rule you added in the last year. Ask the people it affects what they now do differently because of it.
